questions.q: A mutual fund company advertises that its currently available funds have averaged a 12% annual return over the last decade, beating the market. To get this figure, it only counted funds still operating today, excluding the many that underperformed and were quietly shut down or merged away. What statistical error does this illustrate, and how does it affect the reported 12% figure?
choices: Regression to the mean — it deflates the reported average
Confirmation bias — it has no real effect on the figure
Selection bias — it deflates the reported average
Survivorship bias — it inflates the reported average

questions.q: Bertrand's paradox (the chord version): pick a 'random' chord of a circle and ask for the probability that it's longer than the side of the circle's inscribed equilateral triangle. What's the striking result?
choices: The question is meaningless, because circles cannot have chords longer than their inscribed triangle's side
The probability is always exactly 1/3, no matter how the chord is chosen
There's no single answer — different valid methods of choosing a 'random' chord give different correct probabilities (e.g. 1/3, 1/2, or 1/4)
The probability is always exactly 1/2, no matter how the chord is chosen

questions.q: A crime-scene DNA profile matches 1 in 1,000,000 people at random. The suspect's DNA matches. The prosecutor argues this means there is only a 1-in-1,000,000 chance the suspect is innocent. What is wrong with this reasoning?
choices: The DNA test itself must be flawed if this reasoning seems wrong
The reasoning is wrong only if the suspect has an identical twin
Nothing is wrong — 1 in 1,000,000 does mean the suspect is almost certainly guilty
It confuses P(match | innocent) with P(innocent | match) — without knowing the size of the potential suspect pool, the match rate alone doesn't give the probability of guilt

questions.q: Urn A contains 50 red and 50 black balls (known). Urn B contains 100 red and black balls in an unknown ratio. Most people would rather bet on red from Urn A than red from Urn B, AND would also rather bet on black from Urn A than black from Urn B. Is this pair of preferences consistent with holding any single subjective probability for Urn B's colour mix?
choices: Yes — Urn B is also exactly 50/50, so the preferences agree
No — but only because most urns are red-majority
Yes — because both bets are safer with a known urn
No — it's inconsistent with any subjective probability; it reflects pure ambiguity aversion instead

questions.q: The Doomsday Argument reasons that, treating yourself as a random observer among all humans who will ever be born, the roughly 100 billion humans born so far gives a Bayesian reason to doubt that vastly many more humans (say, another 100 trillion) will ever be born — nudging the expected 'doomsday' earlier. Which principle does this argument rest on?
choices: Confirmed trends in declining global fertility rates
The self-sampling assumption: you should reason as if randomly selected from your reference class of observers
Direct astronomical data on asteroid-impact probabilities
The law of large numbers applied to historical birth-rate statistics
